title: The Class Caterpillar
sum: Nora's class keeps a tiny caterpillar named Noodle in a jar, counts the days on a calendar and watches it turn into a monarch butterfly.

cast.d: a seven-year-old second grader who is Jar Helper and loves making signs
cast.look: a seven-year-old girl with two curly puffs of dark hair, a green sweater and a purple marker
a seven-year-old boy with spiky red hair, freckles and an orange hoodie

cast.d: the second-grade teacher who brought the caterpillar from his garden
cast.look: a man with a short black beard, round glasses and a gray sweater vest

cast.d: Nora's mom, who keeps Noodle on the kitchen table for a weekend
cast.look: a woman with curly dark hair tied up and a yellow T-shirt

cast.d: the class caterpillar, later a monarch butterfly
cast.look: a small monarch caterpillar with yellow, black and white stripes; later an orange monarch butterfly with black lines and white dots

p: On Monday, Mr. Lopez carried a big glass jar into class. He set it on the sunny windowsill. The lid had tiny holes for air, and a few green leaves lay on the bottom.
Everyone crowded around, and Sam pressed his nose to the glass. “It's just leaves,” he said.
Mr. Lopez pointed at one leaf. A tiny stripe of yellow, black and white sat on its edge. It was no longer than a grain of rice. Then it wiggled, and Nora gasped. “A caterpillar!”
“A monarch caterpillar,” he said. “It hatched in my garden from an egg as small as a pinhead. It eats only milkweed.”
The new class pet needed a name. Sam's hand shot up first. “Noodle! Because it's long and wiggly.” Nora liked Stripes better, and a boy in the back yelled, “Zippy!”
Mr. Lopez wrote all three names on the board, and all twenty-two kids voted. He drew the tally marks in bundles of five. Four lines stood up, and the fifth went across.
Noodle got two bundles and two more lines. “Five, ten, eleven, twelve!” the class counted. Stripes got one bundle and three more lines, and Zippy got just two.
Nora looked at the tiny caterpillar. It bent in the middle and stretched out again, like a noodle in soup. Fine, the name fit.
Mr. Lopez hung a calendar beside the jar. “Nora, you're Jar Helper this week,” he said. She wrote Day 1 in Monday's box.
On Tuesday, Nora ran straight to the window. She looked in the jar, and then she looked again. There were new holes in the leaves, but no stripes anywhere.
“Noodle's gone!” she said. Sam dropped to the floor and crawled under the desks. Somebody even checked the pencil cups.
Nora checked the lid. It was still on tight, so Noodle had to be inside! She tipped the jar a little and peeked under the leaves, one by one.
Under the biggest leaf, something moved. Noodle was hanging upside down, chewing a brand-new hole. “There you are,” Nora whispered.
“Caterpillars like the bottom of a leaf,” said Mr. Lopez. “Birds can't see them there.” Sam crawled out from under a desk with dust on his nose.
Nora grabbed a marker and made a sign for the jar. It said LOOK UNDER THE LEAVES FIRST! Then she wrote Day 2 on the calendar.

art.s: On a sunny classroom windowsill, a girl in a green sweater tips a big glass jar of milkweed leaves to find a tiny striped caterpillar hanging under the biggest leaf, with a paper calendar and a handmade sign beside the jar.

q.q: Where was Noodle hiding on Tuesday? Draw Noodle and the leaf. Show what Noodle did to the leaf.
look: Noodle upside down under the leaf
q.e: Great looking! Under a leaf, the birds can't see a little caterpillar.

q.q: Why did Sam want to name the caterpillar Noodle?
q.a: Because it was long and wiggly, like a noodle.
q.e: Sam thought it looked long and wiggly. When it bent and stretched, Nora saw it too.

q.q: How many votes did Stripes get?
q.e: One bundle is five. Five and three more make eight.

p: By Friday, Noodle was as long as a paper clip. It ate and ate, until the leaves were full of holes. Tiny dark green balls rolled around the bottom of the jar.
“What are those?” asked Sam. “Poop,” said Mr. Lopez. Sam grinned. “Caterpillar sprinkles.”
Then Mr. Lopez held up the jar. “Who can take care of Noodle this weekend?” Twenty-two hands went up. Nora was Jar Helper, so Noodle went home with her.
He gave Nora a bag of fresh milkweed too. “Noodle eats about four leaves a day now,” he said. “Keep them in the fridge.”
He tucked a folded note into the bag, but Nora didn't see it. She was busy counting out four leaves for Saturday and four for Sunday.
At home, the jar sat in the middle of the kitchen table. Mom bent down close to the glass. “Hello, Noodle,” she said, but Noodle kept chewing.
On Saturday morning, Nora put in four fresh leaves, but Noodle didn't touch them. It sat on the side of the glass, as still as a twig.
Nora's tummy felt tight. She checked the jar before breakfast, after breakfast and after lunch. Noodle never moved. “Is it sick?” she asked Mom.

Mom took the leaf bag out of the fridge. At the bottom was the folded note from Mr. Lopez. Nora read it out loud. “If Noodle stops eating, don't worry. Its skin is getting too tight. Soon it will wiggle out and have a new one.”
Nora let out a long breath. She pulled a chair up to the table and waited. And waited.

After dinner, Noodle began to wiggle. A tiny crack opened behind its head. Noodle pushed forward, and the old skin slid back like a sock coming off. Underneath, the new stripes looked bright and shiny.
Then Noodle turned around and ate the old skin. “Yuck!” said Nora. Mom laughed so hard she had to sit down.

On Sunday, Noodle was hungry again. It ate all four of Sunday's leaves and started on Saturday's too. Before bed, Nora wrote a note for Mr. Lopez: “Noodle got a new skin. Then Noodle ate it.” She taped it to the jar, right under her other sign.

art.s: At a kitchen table in the evening, a girl and her mom lean close to a glass jar where a striped caterpillar crawls forward out of its crumpled old skin.

q.q: Nora packed leaves for Saturday and Sunday. Draw them in two groups, one group for each day. How many leaves in all?
q.e: Four and four make eight. That's a lot of leaves for one little caterpillar!

q.q: Why did Noodle wiggle out of its old skin?
q.e: Noodle grew so fast that the old skin got too tight, like shoes you have grown out of.

q.q: Noodle stopped eating. How did Nora feel? Write one word.
q.e: Her tummy felt tight because she was worried. The note from Mr. Lopez helped her feel better.

p: Nora carried Noodle back to school on Monday. All week Noodle ate, chewing leaves from the tip to the stem. By Thursday it was as long as Nora's pinky finger.
Then, just before home time, Noodle stopped eating. It crawled up the glass and onto the lid. There it spun a little button of silk and hung on with its back end.
On Friday morning, Noodle was hanging upside down with its head curled up. “It looks like a J!” said Sam. It really did.
“Something big will happen today,” said Mr. Lopez. “It happens fast, so we'll take turns watching.” He made a list on the board. Two kids would watch at a time, for half an hour each.
The first pair started at nine o'clock, and Nora and Sam were the fourth pair. Nora watched the clock more than the jar. At last, it was their turn.
Sam made a sign that said SHH! NOODLE IS BUSY. They sat close to the jar and didn't talk. Noodle didn't move either.
Then the J began to straighten. Noodle's body squeezed in and out, like a heartbeat. “Nora,” Sam whispered. “Look!”
“Everybody, come quick!” Nora called, and the whole class crowded around the window. “Don't blink,” said Mr. Lopez.

A split opened near Noodle's head, and something green pushed out. Noodle twisted and wiggled, and the old striped skin slid up toward the lid. Then it dropped off. The whole thing took about three minutes.
Now a green case hung from the lid, with Noodle inside. At first it was soft and lumpy. By lunch it was smooth and shaped like a little lantern. A thin line of gold dots ran around the top.
“It looks like a gumdrop,” said Sam. “Can I eat it?” The whole class shouted, “No!”
“It's called a chrysalis,” said Mr. Lopez, and the class sounded it out together. Kris-uh-lis. Nora wrote the new word in Friday's box, right next to Day 12.

art.s: A class of children crowds around a glass jar on a windowsill where a smooth green chrysalis with gold dots hangs from the lid, a handmade SHH sign taped to the glass and a clock on the wall.

q.q: The first pair watched at 9:00. Each turn was half an hour. Nora and Sam were fourth. What time did their turn start?
q.e: 9:00, 9:30, 10:00, 10:30. The fourth turn started at half past ten.

q.q: Mr. Lopez said, “Don't blink.” What did he mean?
q.e: The change took only about three minutes. One blink, and you might miss it!

q.q: Draw how Noodle changed on Friday. First draw the J. Then draw what was hanging there by lunch.
look: Noodle hanging upside down like a J
a green chrysalis with gold dots
the J first and the chrysalis second
q.e: Two pictures, in order. Now anyone can see how Noodle changed.

p: All Friday afternoon, the chrysalis hung from the lid without eating or moving. “How long until it's a butterfly?” asked Sam. “About ten days,” said Mr. Lopez. “Maybe a few more.”

Nora put her finger on the calendar. She started at Day 12 and counted ten boxes. Her finger stopped on a Monday, Day 22. In that box she wrote two words and a question mark: BUTTERFLY DAY? After all, Mr. Lopez had said “about.”

A chrysalis doesn't need food, so Noodle stayed at school over the weekend. The next week crawled by. Every morning the class checked the jar before they even took off their coats. Green. Still green.
On Thursday, everyone got paper and paint. “Paint on one half only,” said Mr. Lopez. “Then fold it and press.”
Sam painted one big orange wing with four fat dots on it. He used a lot of paint. When he folded the paper and pressed, orange squished out onto his sleeves.
He peeled the paper open. Now there were two wings, and the two sides matched exactly. “Whoa,” said Sam. “I only painted half of that.”
At last it was Monday, Day 22. Everyone ran to the jar, but the chrysalis was still green. The class groaned. “Well,” said Sam, “your question mark was right.”
On Tuesday morning, Nora stopped in the doorway. The chrysalis had turned dark, almost black. “Oh no,” said Sam. “Did it go bad?”
Nora's heart thumped. She got the magnifying glass from the science shelf and held it up to the jar. Through the dark case she could see orange patches and black lines, all folded up small.
“Those are wings!” Nora said. Mr. Lopez leaned in close. “The butterfly is almost ready,” he said. “Now its colors show through the case.”
Nora picked up her marker and drew an arrow from Monday's box to Wednesday's box. At home time she looked back at the jar once more. A little orange showed through, like a night-light left on.

art.s: A girl holds a magnifying glass up to a dark chrysalis with orange wing lines showing through, while a boy with orange paint on his sleeves holds up a folded paper butterfly with matching dots.

q.q: Why did Nora put a question mark after BUTTERFLY DAY?
q.e: Mr. Lopez said “about ten days,” so Nora was not sure. A question mark shows that.

q.q: What did Nora see through the dark chrysalis?
q.e: The butterfly was almost ready, so its wing colors showed through the case.

q.q: Sam painted one wing with four dots, then folded the paper. Draw his butterfly. How many dots are there in all?
q.e: Four and four make eight. Real butterflies match on both sides too!

p: On Wednesday, Nora got to school early. The clock over the door said eight o'clock. She ran to the jar and stopped. The chrysalis hung open at the bottom, empty and clear as plastic wrap.
A butterfly was hanging from it. Its body was fat, and its wings were small and crumpled like wet tissue paper. “Mr. Lopez!” Nora called. “Noodle came out!”
Mr. Lopez came running with his coffee, and they watched together. Little by little, the wings got bigger and flatter. Noodle was pumping them full, like filling a water balloon.
Soon the rest of the class came in. By then the wings were bright orange, with black lines and white dots around the edges. Noodle was a monarch butterfly.
“Let's open the lid!” said Sam. “Not yet,” said Mr. Lopez. “The wings are still soft, and they need about four hours to dry.” Sam flopped onto his desk. Four hours was forever.
Their teacher pointed to the back wings. On each one sat a small black spot. “Those two spots mean he's a boy,” he said.
Sam frowned. “We can't call him Noodle anymore. He isn't wiggly.” Nora looked at the butterfly for a long time. “He's still Noodle,” she said. Nobody argued.
“It's fall now,” said Mr. Lopez. “Soon it will be too cold here for butterflies. Noodle will fly south, maybe all the way to Mexico, where winter is warmer.”

The class watched the clock all morning. They did math and read books, and they peeked at Noodle every time they walked by. When both hands on the clock pointed straight up, Mr. Lopez picked up the jar.
Everyone went out to the garden by the fence. Nora held the jar and lifted the lid. Noodle climbed up onto the rim. His wings opened and closed, once, twice.
Then he flew. Up he went, over the fence and the trees, toward the noon sun. Twenty-two kids waved until they couldn't see him. Nora waved with both arms.
Back inside, Nora drew a butterfly in the box for Day 24. Then she made one last sign and taped it to the empty jar. It said GONE SOUTH FOR THE WINTER.

art.s: In a school garden at noon, children wave as an orange-and-black monarch butterfly flies up from an open glass jar held by a girl in a green sweater, toward the sun above the trees.

q.q: Draw Nora saying goodbye to Noodle. Give her a speech bubble. What does she say?
look: a speech bubble with Nora's words
Nora's face showing how she feels
q.e: What a kind goodbye. Noodle is on his way!

q.q: Noodle came out at 8 o'clock. His wings needed four hours to dry. What time could he fly?
q.e: Nine, ten, eleven, twelve. At 12 o'clock, both clock hands point straight up.

c: Summer here is too hot for him.
Winter here is too cold for him.
The school is too noisy for him.
The garden is too small for him.
q.e: In fall, monarchs fly south to get away from the cold winter.

fin.q: How many days was Noodle with the class, from the day he came to the day he flew away?
fin.e: Noodle came on Day 1 and flew away on Day 24. That's 24 days on the calendar.

fin.q: Which shows Noodle's life in the right order?
fin.e: First a tiny egg, then Noodle the caterpillar, then the green chrysalis, and last the butterfly.
